summary: US export control policy shift (post-Jensen) risks accelerating Huawei's AI hardware ecosystem development
summary_extended: Baker argues that US export control policy — specifically the post-Jensen Huang era shift away from allowing lower-powered Nvidia GPUs into China — represents a grave strategic miscalculation that will accelerate Huawei's AI hardware ecosystem. His reasoning is that Jensen's original approach of permitting limited Nvidia GPU sales to China was deliberately keeping Chinese AI labs dependent on Nvidia silicon, which meant Huawei's competing chips were never deployed at scale and therefore never improved rapidly through real-world usage and iteration. With Chinese AI labs now forced to use Huawei hardware exclusively due to tightened export controls, Baker contends that usage-driven improvement cycles will cause Huawei's chips to advance rapidly — potentially closing the gap with Nvidia far faster than Washington policymakers anticipate. The investment implication is a long-term threat to Nvidia's competitive moat in AI hardware, as a battle-hardened Huawei ecosystem could eventually compete globally, not just within China. Baker frames this as a structural geopolitical risk created by well-intentioned but strategically naive Washington policy, with no near-term resolution in sight.
detail: Baker argues Jensen's policy of allowing less-powerful Nvidia GPUs into China was strategically slowing Huawei's hardware development because Huawei chips weren't being used at scale. Now that Chinese AI labs are forced to use Huawei hardware exclusively, usage will drive rapid improvement. This is framed as a grave national security risk from well-intentioned but misguided Washington policy.
confidence_evidence: Baker makes this argument forcefully and at length, framing it as a structural geopolitical risk with direct investment implications for Nvidia's long-term competitive moat.
